<explanation>
Based on the file structure and README details, you’re looking at a SwiftUI application that follows Clean Architecture principles — dividing the app into Presentation, Business Logic (Interactors), and Data Access (Repositories) layers. Here’s how to create a detailed system design diagram that will capture the project’s architecture accurately:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Presentation Layer: Represented by the UI folder. This includes various SwiftUI views such as CountriesListView, CountryCell, CountryDetailsView, and common UI components like ErrorView and ImageView. Note that these views are largely “dumb” and simply reflect the current state.
   • Business Logic Layer: Represented by the Interactors directory along with centralized state management in AppState (in the Core folder) and supporting components in App.swift and AppDelegate.swift. This layer is responsible for handling user actions, invoking side effects, and updating the state.
   • Data Access Layer: Represented by the Repositories folder that further splits into:
       ▪ Database – implementing local persistence (e.g., CountriesDBRepository and ModelContainer).
       ▪ WebAPI – handling the external REST API (e.g., CountriesWebRepository, ImagesWebRepository, and PushTokenWebRepository).
   • Dependency Injection: Shown by the DependencyInjection folder (with DIContainer and AppEnvironment) that injects required components (state, interactors, repositories) into the view hierarchy.
   • Additional Components: Utilities (helpers like CancelBag, Loadable, Store), Core event handlers (DeepLinksHandler, PushNotificationHandler, and SystemEventsHandler) to manage lifecycle events and deep linking for navigation.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   • The Presentation layer (SwiftUI Views) interacts with the Business Logic layer by dispatching user actions (e.g., onAppear events, button taps) to Interactors.
   • Interactors process these actions by triggering asynchronous operations to fetch data either from the WebAPI or the local Database via the Repositories.
   • The results flow back into the centralized AppState – making it the single source of truth – which is then observed by the SwiftUI views.
   • Dependency Injection is used to seamlessly inject the state and interactors into the view environment using Swift’s property wrappers (@Environment).
   • Utility components and event handlers intercept system events and deep link events to trigger related interactors.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Clean Architecture – separation of concerns into Presentation, Business Logic, and Data Access.
   • Dependency Injection – making the system easily testable and modular.
   • Centralized State Management – a Redux-like approach where AppState holds the entire application state.
   • Asynchronous Data Flow – utilizes Combine’s Publisher for handling asynchronous tasks, in conjunction with async-await based networking.
   • Extensibility – there is a clear separation between DB and Web access, allowing adding or swapping data sources easily.

4. Tailor the Diagram to the Specific Project Type:
   Since this is a full-stack SwiftUI application (albeit client-focused) with clearly delineated architecture layers:
   • Show three major vertical tiers: Presentation (top), Business Logic (middle), and Data Access (bottom).
   • In the Presentation tier, include components like CountriesListView, CountryDetailsView, and common UI views. Indicate that these views are “state-driven” by the AppState.
   • In the Business Logic tier, include the Interactors (CountriesInteractor, ImagesInteractor, UserPermissionsInteractor) alongside the centralized AppState and core system handlers.
   • In the Data Access tier, split it into two sub-components: one for the local Database (CountriesDBRepository, ModelContainer) and one for WebAPI operations. Indicate that these components are used exclusively by Interactors.
   • Also, add a side component for Dependency Injection which flows into both the Business Logic and Presentation layers.

5. Include Visual Elements and Annotations:
   • Label each box clearly with its component name (e.g., “SwiftUI Views – Presentation Layer”, “Interactors – Business Logic Layer”, “Repositories – Data Access Layer”).
   • Use directional arrows to represent data flow:
       – An arrow from SwiftUI Views to Interactors to show user actions triggering business logic.
       – Arrows from Interactors to both AppState (for state updates) and to Repositories to signal data fetch or persistence operations.
       – Arrows from Repositories (both DB and WebAPI) feeding back data into Interactors.
   • Use color coding or distinct shapes to separate:
       – UI (e.g., rounded rectangles in one color),
       – Business logic components (perhaps squares in another color),
       – Data access components (another distinct color)
   • Add annotations to show that dependency injection mediates the passage of AppState and interactors into the view hierarchy.

6. Extra Considerations:
   • Optionally include the testing layer (UnitTests) in the diagram as a separate but connected component to indicate that all functional blocks are fully covered by tests.
   • Indicate how system events (deep linking, push notifications) are intercepted via specific handlers and fed into the respective interactors.
   • Emphasize the use of Combine for asynchronous events in the flow between the Interaction and Data Access layers.

By following these guidelines, you’ll produce a detailed and accurate diagram that clearly captures the separation of concerns within the project as well as the data flow between the presentation, business, and data access layers. This will be a valuable guide for other developers and a strong reference for the overall software architecture. 
</explanation>
